title: Teaching children
hookLine: a man talks out loud in the middle of prayer, and the Prophet teaches him without a single harsh word
tomorrow: what teaches louder than a lecture?

lines: WRONG, IN THE MIDDLE OF PRAYER.
cards: A pencil hits the wall. A nine-year-old shoves his worksheet away: I'm stupid, I can't do this. The next five seconds decide a lot, and the instinct is to get firm.
In Sahih Muslim, a grown man remembers the day he was the one who got it wrong, out loud, in the middle of prayer. And he remembers exactly what the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did next.

teach.h: TALKING IN PRAYER, AND NO SCOLDING.
teach.b: His name is Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam, and he was new to Islam. Someone sneezed during the prayer, and Mu'awiya blessed him, out loud. People glared and slapped their thighs to hush him.
He braced for it. Afterward, he says: I never saw a teacher, before or since, who taught better than him. He didn't scold me, didn't hit me, didn't insult me.
He just explained: this prayer isn't the place for ordinary talk; it's for glorifying God and reciting. A rule, given warmly.

teach.h: A TEACHER WHO MAKES THINGS EASY.
teach.b: In another report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet describes himself: God didn't send me to be harsh, but as a teacher who makes things easy.
And Sahih al-Bukhari has a line any tutor could tape to the desk: make things easy, not hard; give good news, don't drive people away. The Qur'an says why it worked.
In Pickthall's words: "for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee." Gentle isn't soft on the lesson.
Mu'awiya still learned the rule. Gentle is soft on the person. The Arabic for it is rifq.

how: Muslim parents and weekend-school teachers often quote 'make things easy, not hard' and the story of Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam when talking about how to teach children the prayer and the Qur'an.

o: sending children to a school to learn the rules
passing on what you know to the young, patiently
making sure that children obey their elders

games.q: who taught what — tap the pairs.
p: a teacher who makes things easy
make it easy, don't drive away

s: being gentle with a child means letting mistakes slide
Mu'awiya was still taught the rule, just without scolding.
the Prophet described himself as sent as a teacher who makes things easy
that's the report in Sahih Muslim: not harsh, but a teacher who makes things easy.
Qur'an 3:159 says people would have scattered if the Prophet had been harsh
'stern and fierce of heart', and they would have dispersed.

games.q: your daughter recites al-Fatiha at bedtime and gets the same word wrong again. she's tired. what fits today's teaching?
o: say the right word warmly once, praise the rest, and stop for tonight.
have her repeat the whole surah until she says it with no mistakes.
let the mistake go; correcting a tired child will only put her off.
games.why: Mu'awiya still learned the rule, without a harsh word. make it easy, give good news: soft on the person, not on the lesson.

practice: Sit the way you'd sit beside a frustrated child: a little lower, shoulders soft, hands open, next to them rather than across from them.
Stay in that posture and breathe slowly, letting the voice in your head get a little quieter with each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Teaching children: passing on what you know to the young, with patience. The Prophet called himself a teacher sent to make things easy.

orig.note: Arabic: gentleness, kindness in the way a thing is done. one hadith says God is gentle and loves gentleness.

carryVoice: Your line: gently. Soft on the person, never soft on the lesson itself. See you after.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 537: Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam speaks in prayer; 'I never saw a teacher before or after him who taught better; he did not scold me, hit me or revile me'
Sahih Muslim 1478: God did not send me to be harsh, but sent me as a teacher who makes things easy
Sahih al-Bukhari 69: make things easy, not hard; give good news, do not drive people away
